newsitem.title: THAILAND: Lingering property sector woes to hit Thai stocks.
newsitem.headline: Lingering property sector woes to hit Thai stocks.

text.p: Battered Thai stocks will remain in the doldrums until the November 17 general election as concern about cashflow problems at some property firms takes centre stage, market analysts said on Wednesday.

"Right now investors don't have any confidence in the market at all. Rumours that some property developers may have cashflow problems in settling debts with banks and financial firms have worsened the situation," said Songyos Kulvichien, assistant vice president of First Asia Securities.
Thai stocks, now at their lowest in over three years, have fallen nearly 30 percent since January 3.
The stock index finished down 18.45 points at 906.11 on Wednesday, its lowest close since July 27, 1993 when it ended at 893.14.

The market has been sliding since August on worries about political problems faced by the outgoing coalition government of premier Banharn Silpa-archa and an economic slowdown with negligible exports growth, analysts said.
The property sector is facing a slump due to overbuilding and a glut in the prime Bangkok condominium and residential market, they said.
The economic slowdown coupled with the property sector slump had made several property issues the target of rumours about their liquidity positions for some time now, analysts added.
The rumours pushed investors to sell bank and finance company stocks on fears that loan defaults by the property sector would hit performance of financial institutions, they said.

Amid all this, property firm Somprasong Land Plc came under a cloud after the bourse suspended its stocks and police this week issued a warrant of arrest for its president Prasong Panichpakdi on charges of falsifying the firm's financial statements.
The company has many creditors including leading banks and finance companies, analysts said.
Last week, another developer Juldis Develop Plc denied that it was faced with cash flow problems after rumours that it was saddled with debts from Finance One Plc, Thailand's largest finance company.

"Investors are now waiting for a final election poll which is expected to be released in the next two weeks to see which political party would gain most parliamentary seats in order to form a new government," said Songyos.
Somchai Trairattanapirom, vice president of Sitca Investment and Securities, said the current lame-duck administration of caretaker premier Banharn was not in any position to shore up the bourse.

"Sitca has forecast that the market would remain bearish until the general election. The election is the only remedy to the ailing market as it could build up confidence among the investors," he said.
